input: why is booting the page that won't be needed for the longest time the best possible choice? feels arbitrary
expected_output: Belady showed that replacing the page that will be accessed furthest in the future gives the fewest possible cache misses. The reasoning is that all the other pages in the cache will be referred to before that one, so they are more important to keep.

evidence.quote: approach that replaces the page that will be accessed furthest in the future is the optimal policy, resulting in the fewest-possible cache misses.
The reason this is true is simple: you will refer to the other pages before you refer to the one furthest out.
By doing so, you are essentially saying that all the other pages in the cache are more important than the one furthest out.

input: how does the clock algorithm use that one bit to pick which page to evict
expected_output: Hardware sets the bit to 1 whenever a page is read or written, and never clears it; clearing is the OS's job. When a replacement is needed, the OS checks the page under the pointer: if the bit is 1 the page was recently used, so the OS clears it to 0 and moves to the next page. This continues until it finds a page whose bit is 0, meaning it has not been recently used, and that page is replaced.

evidence.quote: Whenever a page is referenced (i.e., read or written), the use bit is set by hardware to 1. The hardware never clears the bit, though (i.e., sets it to 0); that is the responsibility of the OS.

If 1, this implies that page P was recently used and thus is not a good candidate for replacement. Thus, the use bit for P set to 0 (cleared), and the clock hand is incremented to the next page (P + 1).
The algorithm continues until it finds a use bit that is set to 0, implying this page has not been recently used

input: How does the way FIFO picks a page to throw out differ from what LRU does, and why can FIFO evict a page that is used all the time?
expected_output: FIFO evicts whichever page was brought into memory first, no matter how often it has been used, so a page accessed many times still gets kicked out. LRU instead replaces the least-recently-used page, so it looks at access history rather than arrival order.

evidence.quote: FIFO simply can’t determine the importance of blocks: even though page 0 had been accessed a number of times, FIFO still kicks it out, simply because it was the first one brought into memory.
policy replaces the least-recently-used page.
From the figure, you can see how LRU can use history to do better than stateless policies such as Random or FIFO.

input: ram access is 200ns, disk is 5ms, and 99% of accesses hit ram. whats the average access time?
expected_output: Average memory access time is the hit probability times the memory cost plus the miss probability times the disk cost. Here that is 0.99 * 200ns + 0.01 * 5ms = 198ns + 50,000ns = 50,198ns, or about 50 microseconds. Almost all of it comes from the 1% of accesses that go to disk.

evidence.quote: given these values, we can compute the AMAT of a program as follows: AMAT = (PHit · TM) + (PMiss · TD)

where TM represents the cost of accessing memory, TD the cost of accessing disk, PHit the probability of finding the data item in the cache (a hit), and PMiss the probability of not finding the data in the cache (a miss).

evidence.quote: when a replacement occurs, the page on the tail of the queue (the “first-in” page) is evicted.

input: whats that bit the hardware sets when a page gets written and why does the os care
expected_output: It is the modified bit, also called the dirty bit, which the hardware sets any time a page is written. Evicting a dirty page means writing it back to disk, which is expensive, while a clean page can be evicted for free since its frame can just be reused. So the clock algorithm can be changed to scan first for pages that are both unused and clean, and failing that, for unused pages that are dirty.

evidence.quote: the hardware should include a modified bit (a.k.a. dirty bit). This bit is set any time a page is written, and thus can be incorporated into the page-replacement algorithm.
If it has not been modified (and is thus clean), the eviction is free; the physical frame can simply be reused for other purposes without additional I/O.
The reason for this: if a page has been modified and is thus dirty, it must be written back to disk to evict it, which is expensive.
The clock algorithm, for example, could be changed to scan for pages that are both unused and clean to evict first; failing to find those, then for unused pages that are dirty, and so forth.

input: why dont oses just do exact lru all the time? what's so hard about it
expected_output: Perfect LRU needs accounting work on every memory reference, because each access must update a data structure to move that page to the front of the list. Finding the single least-recently-used page by scanning all the access times becomes prohibitively expensive as the number of pages grows.

evidence.quote: To keep track of which pages have been least- and most-recently used, the system has to do some accounting work on every memory reference.
as the number of pages in a system grows, scanning a huge array of times just to find the absolute least-recently-used page is prohibitively expensive.

Specifically, upon each page access (i.e., each memory access, whether an instruction fetch or a load or store), we must update some data structure to move this page to the front of the list (i.e., the MRU side).

input: adding more page frames can only help right? so fifo with 4 frames can't have a lower hit rate than with 3
expected_output: That is not true for FIFO. For some reference streams, going from a cache of 3 to 4 pages makes FIFO's hit rate worse, which is called Belady's Anomaly. LRU avoids this because it has the stack property, where a cache of size N + 1 includes the contents of a cache of size N so hit rate stays the same or improves; FIFO and Random do not obey it.

evidence.quote: In general, you would expect the cache hit rate to increase (get better) when the cache gets larger. But in this case, with FIFO, it gets worse!
a cache of size N + 1 naturally includes the contents of a cache of size N. Thus, when increasing the cache size, hit rate will either stay the same or improve.
FIFO and Random (among others) clearly do not obey the stack property, and thus are susceptible to anomalous behavior.
As it turns out, LRU has what is known as a stack property [M+70].

input: program loops over 20 pages and the cache holds 19, lru should do great here right?
expected_output: No, a loop like this is a worst case for LRU and FIFO. They kick out the older pages, but because the program loops, those older pages are going to be accessed sooner than the pages they prefer to keep. Random actually fares notably better, since it at least achieves a non-zero hit rate.

evidence.quote: This workload, common in many applications (including important commercial applications such as databases [CD85]), represents a worst-case for both LRU and FIFO.

These algorithms, under a looping-sequential workload, kick out older pages; unfortunately, due to the looping nature of the workload, these older pages are going to be accessed sooner than the pages that the policies prefer to keep in cache.
Interestingly, Random fares notably better, not quite approaching optimal, but at least achieving a non-zero hit rate.

input: If the running programs together need more RAM than the machine has and it ends up swapping all the time, what are the OS's options?
expected_output: That situation, where the system is constantly paging, is called thrashing. One approach is to decide not to run a subset of processes, hoping the remaining processes' working sets fit in memory so they can make progress. A more drastic approach is used by some versions of Linux, which run an out-of-memory killer.

evidence.quote: In this case, the system will constantly be paging, a condition sometimes referred to as thrashing [D70].
a system could decide not to run a subset of processes, with the hope that the reduced set of processes working sets (the pages that they are using actively) fit in memory and thus can make progress.
some versions of Linux run an out-of-memory killer when memory is oversubscribed;

input: my box keeps hitting swap constantly and tweaking the eviction algorithm barely helps. what's the realistic fix?
expected_output: Paging to disk is so expensive that the cost of frequent paging is prohibitive, so a smarter algorithm only goes so far. The best solution is often a simple one, even if it is intellectually dissatisfying: buy more memory.

evidence.quote: Because paging to disk is so expensive, the cost of frequent paging is prohibitive. Thus, the best solution to excessive paging is often a simple (if intellectually dissatisfying) one: buy more memory.
However, in many cases the importance of said algorithms has decreased, as the discrepancy between memory-access and disk-access times has increased.
